summary: Collects three memos prepared for ITU-T Study Group 2 about operational decisions in ENUM, the system that maps telephone numbers to Internet addresses. It records the history and context of those choices. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a folder of background notes explaining to a phone-standards group why certain choices were made for linking phone numbers to the Internet.

questions: why does enum use a single domain
subtitle: Why ENUM uses one domain, .ARPA, and RIPE NCC

tldr.problem: ENUM (mapping telephone numbers to Internet addresses in DNS) needed a clear governance model and infrastructure home. The IETF had to decide on one domain, its location, and who would operate it.
tldr.mechanism: Three design memos documented why ENUM uses a single domain (global uniqueness), why it lives in .ARPA (infrastructure stability), and why RIPE NCC operates it (proven reliability and impartiality).
tldr.outcome: These decisions were contributed to ITU-T to explain the technical and governance reasoning, providing the telecommunications standards body with the context needed to work with the IETF on ENUM administration.

today: RFC 3245 is an Informational document that recorded the historical context of ENUM governance decisions. ENUM is still defined by RFC 2916 and operates as described in this document, with e164.arpa administered by RIPE NCC under IETF and ITU cooperation.

sections.title: ENUM and the Need for Governance
sections.content: RFC 3245 contains three memos originally prepared for ITU-T Study Group 2 to explain the IETF's decisions about ENUM (Telephone Number Mapping). ENUM maps the E.164 telephone number system into the DNS, allowing lookups like reverse telephone directories. The memos explain why the IETF settled on single domain, the infrastructure role of .ARPA, and the role of RIPE NCC as its operator. These documents matter because telephone standards and Internet standards had to meet on common ground, and the ITU needed to understand the reasoning.
sections.plainLanguage: The Internet and telephone companies needed to agree on how to store phone numbers on the Internet. This memo explains the three big choices they made.

sections.title: One Domain and One Root
sections.content: The DNS has a fundamental property: each domain name is globally unique, from a single root zone served by well-known root servers. This means any two parties querying the DNS for the same name will end up at the same answer. ENUM needs the same property for telephone numbers. If multiple ENUM trees existed in the DNS, each carrier could assign different meanings to the same country code, routing the same number to different circuits or rejecting it. For a global lookup system, there must be only one place to search. The problem is simple: if storing information in DNS, how does a second party know where the first party stored it without central agreement on one domain?
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine if different post offices used different rules for where to send mail. Everyone needs one shared rule about which post office handles which addresses.

sections.title: .ARPA as Infrastructure Home
sections.content: The .ARPA top-level domain exists for infrastructure uses. Originally created for the DNS transition strategy and reverse mapping of IPv4 addresses (in-addr.arpa), ARPA was formally rationalised as "Address and Routing Parameters Area" and placed under IAB supervision. It is the designated home for protocol-infrastructure domains like IPv6 reverse mapping (ip6.arpa). Placing ENUM in .ARPA meant it would sit alongside other core Internet infrastructure rather than creating a new top-level domain, which would have been slower to establish and operationally harder to maintain. ARPA has strict stability requirements inherited from root zone operations, ensuring global reliability.
sections.plainLanguage: Special infrastructure like phone number lookup lives in a special part of the Internet name system designed for critical services, not in the commercial parts.

sections.title: RIPE NCC as Operator
sections.content: Operating e164.arpa requires the same high standards as root nameservers: reliability, security, fairness and impartiality. The IAB selected criteria for the operator: a history of reliable DNS operations, respect in the community, relevant technical skills, fairness, and non-profit status (to remove profit-driven incentives to exploit the registry). All three regional IP registries (RIRs) met these criteria. RIPE NCC was chosen for its greater DNS experience and its location in a neutral legal jurisdiction. Once a country code's subdomain is assigned to an appropriately-designated national entity, that entity administers its own subdomain without further involvement from the IETF, IAB or ITU.
sections.plainLanguage: One trusted organization with a long track record of handling Internet infrastructure gets to run the service. National phone authorities can manage their own country's listings.

sections.title: Documentation and Future Use
sections.content: These memos were provided to ITU-T because international telecommunications governance required documentation of why these decisions were made. By explaining the reasoning to a standards body that manages telephone numbering, the IETF made sure both communities understood the technical necessities and shared purpose. The memos also show how the IAB and IETF coordinate with ICANN and national authorities. The IAB and RIPE NCC have published procedures for registering country-code subdomains, which are expected to evolve as experience accumulates. This joint documentation effort ensured that telephone and Internet standards could work together on the same infrastructure.
sections.plainLanguage: The Internet engineers explained their thinking to the phone standards people so everyone could work together smoothly.
